name.text: MQH - Determine the Convergence or Divergence of an Improper Integral

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the Integral below and determine if it converges or diverges.

Note: \( \infty\) is entered as inf and \( -\infty\) is entered as minf.

\( \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}} \, dx =\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

Therefore, the integral is [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

To evaluate the integral \( \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}} \, dx\), we first check for Convergence or Divergence of the integral.

Since \(x = {@lower_limit@}\) is the lower bound of the integral, \( \displaystyle \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}}\) is undefined at \(x = {@lower_limit@}\).

Therefore, we’ll need to replace \({@lower_limit@}\) with a parameter \(t\) as follows,

Rewrite the integral as an improper integral:

\( \qquad \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}} \, dx = \lim_{t \to {@lower_limit@}^{+}} \int_{t}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}}\, dx\).

Now, we integrate \( \displaystyle \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}}\) with respect to \(x\):

\( \qquad \displaystyle \begin{align} \int \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}}\, dx &= {@num@} \cdot \frac{x^{{@-power@} + 1}}{{@-power@} + 1} \\ & = {@num@} \cdot \frac{x^{{@-power+1@}}}{ \displaystyle {@-power+1@}} \\ &= {@new_indef@} \end{align} \)

Thus, \(\displaystyle \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}} \, dx = \lim_{t \to {@lower_limit@}^{+}} \left[ {@new_indef@} \right]_{t}^{{@upper_limit@}}\)

Substitute the limits: \(\displaystyle \lim_{t \to {@lower_limit@}^{+}} \left( \displaystyle {@ta@} \right) \to {@ta_1@}\).

\( \implies \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}} \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}} \, dx \to {@ta_1@}\).

Therefore, the integral is \(\displaystyle \text{@ta_2@}\)

hint.text:
Hint: Before integrating, try simplifying the expression \( \displaystyle \frac{{@num@}}{{@den1@}{@den2@}}\) by writing \( \sqrt{x} \) as \( \displaystyle x^{{@1/2@}} \), and then express the entire fraction as a power of \( x \).

This will make it easier to apply the power rule for integration.

Hint: Now that you've simplified the integrand to \(\displaystyle {@fx@}\) , recall that the integral of \( x^n \) is \( \displaystyle \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \), as long as \( n \neq -1 \). Use this rule to find the antiderivative.

Hint: As you evaluate the integral from \( {@lower_limit@} \) to \( {@upper_limit@} \), notice that \(\displaystyle {@fx@}\) becomes undefined at \( x = 0 \).

This suggests the possibility of divergence. Think about whether the function has a finite area under the curve at \( x = 0 \). Can you conclude whether the integral converges or diverges?
